\section[\hi{बोलना}]{\hi{बोलना} (bolnā) — \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} your first full verb}

\label{lesson:HI-C05-bolna}



\begin{quote}
Until now, \textquotedblleft{}to be.\textquotedblright{} Here is a verb that \emph{does} something — and it comes in a shape you'll see on every Hindi verb.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\hi{ब}} (\emph{ba}) + \textbf{\hi{ो}} (the \emph{o}-mātrā) $\to$ \textbf{\hi{बो}} (\emph{bo}); \textbf{\hi{ल}} (\emph{la}); \textbf{\hi{ना}} (\emph{nā}). Read \textbf{\hi{बो}·\hi{ल}·\hi{ना}} $\to$ \emph{bolnā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{बोलना}} (\emph{bolnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}) is a native Indo-Aryan verb (from Prakrit \emph{bolla-}, \textquotedblleft{}to utter\textquotedblright{}). Notice its ending: \textbf{-\hi{ना}} (\emph{-nā}). \textbf{Every} Hindi verb, named in the dictionary, ends in \emph{-nā} — it is the infinitive marker, Hindi's \textquotedblleft{}to \_\_\_\textquotedblright{}: \emph{bol-nā} \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} \emph{cal-nā} \textquotedblleft{}to move\textquotedblright{} (you met it in \emph{caltā hūṁ}), \emph{mil-nā} \textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{} (from \emph{milenge}). Strip the \emph{-nā} and you have the \textbf{stem} (\emph{bol-}) that takes all the other endings.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: stem + ending}]
The stem \emph{bol-} is where the action lives; endings pin down who and when: \emph{bol-tā} (speaking, m.), \emph{bol-tī} (speaking, f.), \emph{bol-o} (speak!, familiar command). You will build every tense by adding to a stem like this.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\hi{ब} (\emph{ba}) + \hi{ो} (the \emph{o}-mātrā) $\to$ \hi{बो} (\emph{bo}); \hi{ल} (\emph{la}); \hi{ना} (\emph{nā}). Read \hi{बो}·\hi{ल}·\hi{ना} $\to$ \emph{bolnā}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bolnā\textquotedblright{}
  \item the infinitive marker every Hindi verb ends in (\emph{-nā})
  \item three \emph{-nā} verbs you now know (\emph{bolnā, calnā, milnā})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What ending does every Hindi infinitive carry, and what is \emph{bolnā}'s stem? (\emph{-nā}; the stem is \emph{bol-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{रहना}]{\hi{रहना} (rahnā) — \textquotedblleft{}to live, to stay\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C05-rahna}



\begin{quote}
A second verb, so you can say where you live — and see the \emph{stem + ending} machine work all over again.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\hi{र}} (\emph{ra}) + \textbf{\hi{ह}} (\emph{ha}) + \textbf{\hi{ना}} (\emph{nā}) $\to$ \textbf{\hi{रहना}} (\emph{rahnā}). The familiar infinitive \textbf{-\hi{ना}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{रहना}} (\emph{rahnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to live, to remain, to stay\textquotedblright{}) is from Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{रह्}} (\emph{rah-}, \textquotedblleft{}to remain, be left\textquotedblright{}). It covers both \textquotedblleft{}reside\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}keep on\textquotedblright{}: \emph{maiṁ Dillī meṁ rahtā hūṁ} (\textquotedblleft{}I live in Delhi\textquotedblright{}), \emph{ṭhīk rahnā} (\textquotedblleft{}stay well\textquotedblright{} — a warm sign-off). Stem \emph{rah-} + \emph{-tā/-tī} + \emph{honā}, exactly like \emph{bolnā}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} comes after the noun}]
\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{दिल्ली} \hi{में} \hi{रहता} \hi{हूँ}} (\emph{maiṁ Dillī meṁ rahtā hūṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}I live in Delhi\textquotedblright{}). The little word \textbf{\hi{में}} (\emph{meṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{}) sits \textbf{after} Delhi, not before — Hindi uses \textbf{post}positions where English uses prepositions. \textquotedblleft{}Delhi-in I live.\textquotedblright{} The verb, as ever, is last.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\hi{र} (\emph{ra}) + \hi{ह} (\emph{ha}) + \hi{ना} (\emph{nā}) $\to$ \hi{रहना}. The familiar infinitive -\hi{ना}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY (m.): \emph{maiṁ Dillī meṁ rahtā hūṁ}  ·  (f.): \emph{… rahtī hūṁ}{]}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the root (\emph{rah-} \textquotedblleft{}to remain\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{Say it:} where \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} (\emph{meṁ}) sits — after the noun, not before
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I live in Delhi,\textquotedblright{} and note what is odd (to English ears) about the word \textquotedblleft{}in.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Maiṁ Dillī meṁ rahtā/rahtī hūṁ}; \emph{meṁ} \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} comes \textbf{after} Delhi — a postposition.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{करना}]{\hi{करना} (karnā) — \textquotedblleft{}to do,\textquotedblright{} the most useful verb in Hindi}

\label{lesson:HI-C05-karna}



\begin{quote}
One verb powers a thousand phrases — and its root already sits inside a word you learned back in Chapter 1.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\hi{क}} (\emph{ka}) + \textbf{\hi{र}} (\emph{ra}) + \textbf{\hi{ना}} (\emph{nā}) $\to$ \textbf{\hi{करना}} (\emph{karnā}). Simple letters, enormous reach.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{करना}} (\emph{karnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to do, to make\textquotedblright{}) is from Sanskrit \textbf{√\hi{कृ}} (\emph{√kṛ}, \textquotedblleft{}to do, make\textquotedblright{}) — one of the most productive roots in all of Sanskrit, and from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}er-}. You have met its family already:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{कर्म}} (\emph{karma}) = \textquotedblleft{}a thing \textbf{done},\textquotedblright{} an action and its consequence.
  \item \textbf{\hi{नमस्कार}} (\emph{namaskār}) = \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{making} of a bow\textquotedblright{} (\emph{namas} + \emph{kār}) — the greeting from Chapter 1.
  \item \textbf{\hi{संस्कृत}} (\emph{saṃskṛta}, \textquotedblleft{}Sanskrit\textquotedblright{}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{put together}, perfected.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

So \emph{karnā} is the everyday face of the root behind \emph{karma}, \emph{namaskār}, and the name \emph{Sanskrit} itself.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \hi{करना} makes verbs out of anything}]
Hindi builds countless verbs as \textbf{noun + \hi{करना}}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{काम} \hi{करना}} (\emph{kām karnā}) = \textquotedblleft{}work-do\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to work}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{kām}, \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\hi{बात} \hi{करना}} (\emph{bāt karnā}) = \textquotedblleft{}talk-do\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}to converse\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\hi{इंतज़ार} \hi{करना}} (\emph{intazār karnā}) = \textquotedblleft{}to wait\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

So \emph{maiṁ kām kartā hūṁ} = \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} (lit. \textquotedblleft{}I work-do am\textquotedblright{}). Learn \emph{karnā} and you unlock a whole grammar of \textquotedblleft{}do-verbs.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\hi{क} (\emph{ka}) + \hi{र} (\emph{ra}) + \hi{ना} (\emph{nā}) $\to$ \hi{करना}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}karnā\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} (m./f.) — \emph{maiṁ kām kartā hūṁ / kartī hūṁ}
  \item the Chapter 1 word that shares its root (\emph{namaskār} — the \textquotedblleft{}making\textquotedblright{} of a bow)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Sanskrit root is \emph{karnā} from, and name two words built on it. (\emph{√kṛ} \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{}; any two of \emph{karma}, \emph{namaskār}, \emph{Sanskrit}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{बोलता} \hi{हूँ}, \hi{बोलती} \hi{हूँ}, \hi{बोलते} \hi{हैं}]{\hi{बोलता} \hi{हूँ} (boltā hūṁ) — one stem, and the two things Hindi makes it agree with}

\label{lesson:HI-C05-bolta-hun}



\begin{quote}
You have the stem \emph{bol-}. This lesson is the machine that turns any stem into a sentence about what someone \emph{does} — and it is the single biggest piece of leverage in this book so far, because it fits every verb you will ever meet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \hi{बोलना} — the infinitive, and how to strip \emph{-nā} to get the stem.
  \item \hi{हूँ} — \textquotedblleft{}I am,\textquotedblright{} the verb this template leans on.
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: stem + -tā/-tī/-te + honā}]
To say what someone does \emph{in general}, Hindi builds three pieces in a row: the \textbf{stem}, a \textbf{participle ending}, and the \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} verb}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{who} & \textbf{the pieces} & \textbf{the whole thing} \\
\midrule
I (a man) & \textbf{-\hi{ता}} \emph{-tā} + \textbf{\hi{हूँ}} \emph{hūṁ} & \textbf{\hi{बोलता} \hi{हूँ}} \emph{boltā hūṁ} \\
I (a woman) & \textbf{-\hi{ती}} \emph{-tī} + \textbf{\hi{हूँ}} \emph{hūṁ} & \textbf{\hi{बोलती} \hi{हूँ}} \emph{boltī hūṁ} \\
\hi{आप} \emph{āp} (you, respectful) & \textbf{-\hi{ते}} \emph{-te} + \textbf{\hi{हैं}} \emph{haiṁ} & \textbf{\hi{बोलते} \hi{हैं}} \emph{bolte haiṁ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Strip \emph{-nā}, add the ending, add \emph{honā}. That is the whole rule, and it does not change from verb to verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the two agreements, and why they are two}]
This is the part worth slowing down for, because Hindi is doing \textbf{two separate jobs at once} and a beginner naturally expects one.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{-\hi{ता} / -\hi{ती} / -\hi{ते}} agrees with \textbf{gender and number}. It does not care who is speaking. A woman says \emph{boltī} whether she is talking about herself or being addressed.
  \item \textbf{\hi{हूँ} / \hi{है} / \hi{हैं}} agrees with \textbf{person}. It does not care about gender. \emph{Hūṁ} is \textquotedblleft{}I am\textquotedblright{} for a man and a woman alike.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{boltī hūṁ} is not one ending chosen from a list of six. It is two choices made independently and then set side by side — feminine on the participle, first-person on the verb. Once you treat them as two dials rather than one, the whole present tense stops needing to be memorised.

English does this too, and hides it: \emph{\textquotedblleft{}I am speaking\textquotedblright{}} is also participle plus \emph{to be}. Hindi simply puts the \emph{to be} last, where Hindi always puts its verbs.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY (m.): \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{} — \emph{boltā hūṁ}{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY (f.): \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{} — \emph{boltī hūṁ}{]}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}you (respectful) speak\textquotedblright{} — \emph{āp bolte haiṁ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} which of the two endings changed when you switched from a man to a woman, and which one did not (\emph{-tā}$\to$\emph{-tī} changed; \emph{hūṁ} did not)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Hindi's present habitual makes two agreements at once. Name what each of the two pieces agrees with. (\emph{-tā/-tī/-te} agrees with gender and number; \emph{hūṁ/hai/haiṁ} agrees with person.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोलता} \hi{हूँ}]{\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोलता} \hi{हूँ} (maiṁ hindī boltā hūṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}I speak Hindi\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C05-main-hindi-bolta-hun}



\begin{quote}
Your first complete, moving sentence — subject, object, and a verb that \emph{acts}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\hi{हिंदी}} (\emph{hindī}): \textbf{\hi{ह}} (\emph{ha}) + \textbf{\hi{ि}}$\to$\textbf{\hi{हि}} + the \emph{anusvāra} \textbf{\hi{ं}} + \textbf{\hi{दी}} (\emph{dī}). And \textbf{\hi{बोलता}} (\emph{boltā}) = the stem \emph{bol-} + \textbf{-\hi{ता}} (\emph{-tā}), the present-habitual, masculine.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोलता} \hi{हूँ}} = \textbf{\hi{मैं}} (\emph{maiṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\hi{हिंदी}} (\emph{hindī}, \textquotedblleft{}Hindi,\textquotedblright{} the object) + \textbf{\hi{बोलता}} (\emph{boltā}, \textquotedblleft{}speak,\textquotedblright{} m.) + \textbf{\hi{हूँ}} (\emph{hūṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}am\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I Hindi speaking am}.\textquotedblright{} Verb-frame last, exactly as always.

The name \textbf{\hi{हिंदी}} itself is a traveller: from \textbf{\hi{सिन्धु}} (\emph{sindhu}, the river Indus) $\to$ Persian \emph{hind} (the land past that river) $\to$ \emph{hindī} (\textquotedblleft{}of Hind\textquotedblright{}). The same \emph{sindhu} gave Greek \emph{Indos} $\to$ English \textbf{India}, \textbf{Indus}, \textbf{Hindu}. The language is named, at two removes, after a river.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the frame you already have}]
The verb here is the present habitual — \textbf{stem + -tā/-tī/-te + honā} — which \hi{बोलता} \hi{हूँ} built one lesson ago. Nothing about it is new; this sentence is the first place you get to \emph{use} it on a real object.

What is new is the word order: \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोलता} \hi{हूँ}} puts the object \emph{before} the verb frame, so the sentence ends on \emph{hūṁ}. Hindi's verb goes last, always.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY (m.): \emph{maiṁ hindī boltā hūṁ}  ·  (f.): \emph{maiṁ hindī boltī hūṁ}{]}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}you (resp.) speak Hindi\textquotedblright{} — \emph{āp hindī bolte haiṁ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the river hidden in the word \emph{hindī} (\emph{sindhu}, the Indus)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Build \textquotedblleft{}I speak Hindi\textquotedblright{} as a woman, and name the river behind \emph{hindī}. (\emph{Maiṁ hindī boltī hūṁ}; the \emph{Sindhu}/Indus.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 5 — The first verbs}

\label{lesson:HI-C05-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Three verbs, one engine — build real sentences about yourself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{How to answer — build the sentences}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I speak Hindi\textquotedblright{} (m./f.) — \emph{maiṁ hindī boltā/boltī hūṁ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I live in Delhi\textquotedblright{} — \emph{maiṁ Dillī meṁ rahtā/rahtī hūṁ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} — \emph{maiṁ kām kartā/kartī hūṁ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}you (resp.) speak Hindi\textquotedblright{} — \emph{āp hindī bolte haiṁ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — the engine}]
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the ending every infinitive carries (\emph{-nā})
  \item the two agreements in a present sentence (\emph{-tā/-tī/-te} for gender/number; \emph{hūṁ/hai/haiṁ} for person)
  \item where the verb sits, and where \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} sits (verb last; \emph{meṁ} after the noun)
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bolnā} \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{} (Prakrit \emph{bolla-})
  \item \emph{rahnā} \textquotedblleft{}to live\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{rah-} \textquotedblleft{}to remain\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{karnā} \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{√kṛ} — the root of \emph{karma}, \emph{namaskār}, \emph{Sanskrit}
  \item \emph{hindī} $\leftarrow$ \emph{sindhu}, the river Indus
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In one breath, tell me your language, your city, and your work in Hindi (as a woman). (\emph{Maiṁ hindī boltī hūṁ. Maiṁ … meṁ rahtī hūṁ. Maiṁ kām kartī hūṁ.})
\end{tcolorbox}
